transcript: Here's my take on the brand new Hamlet movie starring Riz Ahmed. And I'm wearing my “alas poor Yorick” hat in honor of the fact that it was cut from this movie. Alas, poor Yorick indeed. This new version is set in modern day London, focusing on an Indian family whose “kingdom” is a controversial real estate empire, which maps onto Shakespeare's text pretty harmoniously as far as I can tell. I mean, when it comes to the strategic incorporation of Indian culture and language, I don't know if I can speak to it with nuance from my perspective, but it seemed to work pretty well. I especially appreciated reimagining Fortinbras’s army as the occupants of a tent city that was displaced by Elsinore. And Hamlet's “how all occasions do inform against me” speech lands a lot more powerfully because there's this sting of betrayal where he realizes that his family, in their search for status and power, has harmed the disadvantaged people in their own community. Next, I have to address the biggest concern I had in my reaction to the trailer, which I noticed included a lot of faux Shakespeare; lines that were meant to sound kind of like Shakespeare, but were written for the film. And I don't object to that kind of practice on principle It's just very difficult to do it well. But it turns out it's not that prevalent in the movie itself. The majority of the dialogue was taken straight from Shakespeare. And the rest of it mostly functioned like connective tissue or exposition to fill in the little gaps left by the heavily abridged script, which was fine with me. They also did a lot of repurposing lines that were from the play but spoken by other characters in different contexts. Like they cut Horatio and redistributed a lot of his lines to Ophelia and Laertes, which actually added a lot of dimension to Hamlet's relationship with both of them. I especially like the idea of having Laertes and Hamlet be friends at the beginning It was a little hit or miss, but most of the cuts and reordering of scenes and most of the interpretive choices that came along with them felt reasonably logical and coherent, sometimes even very insightful. The big exception though, was that they really rushed through that final act. Cutting the mad scene, cutting the Grave Digger. Just the turnaround from Hamlet's banishment felt super quick, which made his arc feel less satisfying. More frustrating though, is that stripping the plot down to its bare bones components made the whole movie feel kind of one-note. Some of that is the direction, I think, where it gets caught in this generalized sense of brooding intensity. But I do also think that a lot of the emotional nuance and dynamic texture from the play wound up on the cutting room floor. Still though, even if the viewing experience was a bit of a mixed bag this adaptation has a lot of great ideas and makes for a respectable addition to a long line of imperfect Hamlet movies.
